title: Memory, Materials and the Built Environment
central_proposition: Encounters with building materials in the built environment constitute confrontations with the past, mediated by individual and cultural memory, leading to an intuitive temporal self-location and shaping our understanding of place.

concept_definitions.name: Memory
concept_definitions.definition: The way that the past invests the present and the way the present addresses the past.

concept_definitions.name: Building materials
concept_definitions.definition: Both construction materials and all the other materials manifest in the built environment.

concept_definitions.name: Material quality
concept_definitions.definition: Affective, interpretive and associative responses to materials, encompassing visible, inner, and associative aspects.

concept_definitions.name: Material literacy
concept_definitions.definition: A broad sensitivity to materials and their diverse meanings.

concept_definitions.name: Age-value (Riegl)
concept_definitions.definition: Attributed to every artifact without regard to its original significance and purpose, as long as it reveals the passage of a considerable period of time.

concept_definitions.name: Historical value (Riegl)
concept_definitions.definition: Localized historical memories a building contains.

argument_structure: The paper critiques existing 'layer images' of time and the overemphasis on historical events in memory studies, proposing a focus on the perceptible surface manifestations of pastness in materials. It argues that materials mediate memory and temporalize individuals through three mechanisms: culturally transmitted associative meanings, intuitive evaluation of physical properties, and the 'reading' of materials for relative oldness (age-value). It uses examples like concrete's association with totalitarianism and Riegl's concept of age-value to illustrate how materials shape our temporal orientation and the 'feel' of places.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: Materials, through their physical properties (e.g., hardness, durability, signs of wear/patina) and culturally mediated associative meanings (derived from historical usage, narratives, and ethical judgments), trigger individual and collective memory processes. These processes enable an intuitive 'reading' of materials, leading to estimations of their relative age and the construction of temporal frameworks. This temporalization of space, in turn, locates the individual within a relational temporal complex and contributes to the affective and atmospheric 'feel' of the built environment.

findings.antecedent: Encounters with building materials in the built environment
findings.mechanism: We observe pastness in the built environment, instinctively undertake relative dating, and, as a result, temporally locate ourselves in relation to the space and the space in relation to ourselves.
findings.quote: This essay rethinks the interrelation between materials and memory, asking: how do our encounters with materials in the built environment confront us with the past
findings.empirical_support_cited: conceptual argument based on existing theories and observations

findings.antecedent: Building materials (construction materials and all other materials in the built environment)
findings.consequent: Individual's understanding of place and sense of temporal orientation
findings.mechanism: Materials mediate memory and temporalize the individual, locating us in time as well as space.
findings.quote: building materials [...] are essential to an individual's understanding of place and sense of temporal orientation.
findings.empirical_support_cited: conceptual argument based on existing theories and observations

findings.mechanism: Our responses to materials are determined by our own past encounters (individual memory) and culturally transmitted associative meanings (cultural memory).
findings.quote: our encounters with building materials are mediated by memory
findings.empirical_support_cited: conceptual argument based on existing theories and observations

findings.mechanism: They transmit meanings, information, and attitudes about the past in important ways.
findings.empirical_support_cited: conceptual argument based on existing theories and observations

findings.consequent: Temporalises the individual in it (locates us in time as well as space)
findings.mechanism: This occurs through encounters with materials as multifaceted cultural memory processes.
findings.quote: the built environment temporalises the individual in it – that is, that the built environment locates us in time as well as in space.
findings.empirical_support_cited: conceptual argument based on existing theories and observations

findings.consequent: Their 'meaning' is a question of memory
findings.mechanism: Our responses are determined by our own past encounters with materials and by culturally transmitted associative meanings.
findings.quote: our understanding of what materials “mean” is a question of memory insofar as our responses to materials are determined at once by our own encounters with materials in the past as well as by culturally transmitted associative meanings
findings.empirical_support_cited: conceptual argument based on existing theories and observations

findings.consequent: Ability to evaluate their physical properties and characteristics (e.g., hardness, durability, age)
findings.mechanism: This capacity draws on both our past experiences with materials (individual memory) and received knowledge (collective semantic memory) about them.
findings.quote: our situated responses to materials incorporate a keen (although not always accurate) ability to evaluate their physical properties and characteristics: this capacity likewise draws both on our past experiences with materials and received knowledge (collective semantic memory) about them.
findings.empirical_support_cited: conceptual argument based on existing theories and observations

findings.antecedent: Reading materials in our immediate physical environments
findings.mechanism: All conscious encounters with physical environments engender the construction of temporal frameworks based on the relative oldness/newness of different elements within it.
findings.quote: the way that we “read” materials in our immediate physical environments temporalises our experience of space, such that all conscious encounters with physical environments engender the construction of temporal frameworks on the basis of the relative oldness/newness of the different elements within it.
findings.empirical_support_cited: conceptual argument based on existing theories and observations

findings.mechanism: Such meanings emerge in situated contexts and only as a result of particular 'routinised patterns of interpretation'.
findings.quote: such meanings emerge in situated contexts and only as a result of particular “routinised patterns of interpretation”
findings.empirical_support_cited: conceptual argument based on existing theories and observations

findings.consequent: Most closely associated with historical eras and political regimes
findings.mechanism: This results from their being the most ostensible visible manifestation of an era or regime, and the frequency with which the association is mediated in communicative exchanges and cultural texts.
findings.quote: facing materials are particularly prone to becoming the materials most closely associated with historical eras and political regimes.
findings.empirical_support_cited: conceptual argument based on existing theories and observations

findings.consequent: Meanings derived from at least two memory sources
findings.mechanism: These sources are individual memories of past encounters and cultural memory (discursively acquired information about properties, uses, contexts, associations, and connotations).
findings.quote: the meanings of materials derive from at least two memory sources: 1) individual memories of our encounters with specific materials in the past and 2) cultural memory
findings.empirical_support_cited: conceptual argument based on existing theories and observations

findings.antecedent: Materials revealing 'the passage of a considerable period of time' (age-value)
findings.mechanism: This discernment is based on perceptible surface manifestations of pastness (corrosion, patina, wear/tear, incompleteness, dissolution of form/color) and does not require specialist knowledge.
findings.quote: everyone intuitively understands the criteria according to which oldness is inferred. Although Riegl does not state precisely what those criteria are or whence they derive, he does note some of the indicators of oldness.
findings.empirical_support_cited: conceptual argument based on existing theories and observations

findings.consequent: Facilitate the temporalising function of the material environment
findings.mechanism: Through the attribution of relative age values to various elements, the material environment achieves the illusion of simultaneously accommodating the nonsimultaneous, inserting us into a relational temporal complex.
findings.quote: our ability to “read” the (relative) oldness of materials means that materials facilitate the temporalising function of the material environment
findings.empirical_support_cited: conceptual argument based on existing theories and observations

findings.antecedent: Materials' associative meanings and perceived oldness/newness
findings.consequent: Shapes how a place feels (affective, associative, atmospheric experience)
findings.mechanism: Textural complexity derived from material diversity also means temporal complexity, which plays a crucial role in making spaces stimulating and pleasant.
findings.quote: the way a place feels is shaped by the materials of the various elements in it both on account of the associative meanings they carry and their perceived oldness/newness.
findings.empirical_support_cited: conceptual argument based on existing theories and observations

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: The influence of individual past encounters versus culturally transmitted associative meanings on material perception and evaluation can be empirically disentangled.
The accuracy and consistency of intuitive relative dating of materials in the built environment can be measured across different cultural contexts.
The perceived temporal complexity of a space, derived from material diversity, correlates with subjective ratings of interest and enjoyment and physiological markers of engagement.
Changes in cultural narratives surrounding a material will lead to shifts in its historical associative meanings and the 'feel' of spaces where it is prominently used.
bridge_warrants: Connects architectural theory (e.g., Rasmussen, Pallasmaa, Munteán) with memory studies.
Integrates semiotic and phenomenological approaches to understanding material meanings.
Applies Riegl's concept of 'age-value' to cultural memory studies, highlighting intuitive temporal discernment.
Draws parallels between Walter Benjamin's archaeological metaphor of memory and the 'layers of time' in the built environment.
Relates to Reinhard Koselleck's concept of 'the simultaneity of the nonsimultaneous' in understanding temporal dimensions of space.
methodological_critiques: Critiques existing 'layer images' of time for distracting from perceptible surface-level manifestations of pastness.
Critiques architectural scholarship for historically underplaying architectural experience and meaning-making, instead focusing on historical styles, utility, strength, and architects' intentions.
Critiques mainstream cultural memory studies for an overemphasis on extraordinary events and historical specificities, neglecting the less precise ways the past invests the present in everyday life.
Critiques the reduction of the built environment to a mere backdrop for events, arguing for its active role in memory processes.
model_structure: The paper proposes a conceptual framework where building materials act as central mediators and facilitators of cultural memory processes. This framework posits that materials, through their physical properties and culturally conditioned meanings, enable individuals to intuitively 'read' pastness and relative age in the built environment. This 'reading' then contributes to the temporal orientation of the individual within space and shapes the affective 'feel' of places, moving beyond event-centric or style-centric interpretations.
limitations: Acknowledges that associative material quality is highly subjective and personal, though also culturally dependent.
Notes that the historical accuracy of associations between materials and historical eras/regimes is secondary to predominant cultural narratives.

paper_metadata.crossref_abstract:
Abstract
This essay rethinks the interrelation between materials and memory, asking: how do our encounters with materials in the built environment confront us with the past and what is the role of memory in such encounters? It argues that encounters with building materials constitute confrontations with the past, as we observe pastness in the built environment, instinctively undertake relative dating, and, as a result, temporally locate ourselves in relation to the space and the space in relation to ourselves. Integrating a key strand of architectural theory – attention to building materials and the material environment – into memory studies, the essay also proposes that the meanings of building materials are mediated by memory and that building materials themselves mediate (cultural) memory. By focusing on materials rather than events or architectural styles, it exposes the multiple and multifaceted cultural memory processes inherent in our everyday engagement with materials.
